query: For high-entropy alloys intended for aerospace fasteners, what single intervention could improve the combination of mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a moderate amount (around 5–10 wt%) of molybdenum (Mo) into a high-entropy alloy (HEA) composition will enhance its mechanical durability, reduce room-temperature creep, and improve its corrosion resistance for aerospace fastener applications.
generation.material_initial_state: A base HEA alloy (e.g. a CrCoNiFe-based alloy) without Mo addition, processed via conventional casting or additive manufacturing methods.
generation.intervention: Add 5–10 wt% Mo into the alloy during processing (e.g. via vacuum arc melting or directed energy deposition) to modify its composition.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature operation with exposure to corrosive environments (such as 3.5 wt% NaCl solution) and mechanical loading typical for aerospace fasteners; standard sample fabrication and heat-treatment conditions are assumed.
generation.structural_mediator: The Mo addition is expected to increase lattice distortion and promote local chemical ordering as well as refinement or stabilization of grain boundaries, thereby impeding dislocation motion and retarding creep.
generation.mechanism: Mo induces a solution-strengthening effect and may promote the formation of fine, Mo-rich secondary features that act as barriers to dislocation movement. This results in improved yield strength and durability. Simultaneously, Mo enhances the corrosion resistance by stabilizing the passivating oxide layers on the alloy surface.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated base alloy, the Mo-modified HEA is predicted to exhibit higher yield and tensile strengths, reduced creep deformation at room temperature under sustained load, and better corrosion performance (e.g., higher corrosion potential and lower corrosion current density).
generation.baseline: The untreated HEA (without Mo) which has demonstrated relatively lower mechanical strength, higher room-temperature creep displacement, and inferior corrosion resistance.
generation.boundary: Improvements are expected within a limited Mo concentration range; excessive Mo may lead to excessive brittleness or formation of unwanted secondary phases. The beneficial effects are also dependent on consistent processing and heat-treatment parameters.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence suggests Mo can improve both mechanical and corrosion properties, the exact magnitude of improvement in room-temperature creep resistance and overall durability is uncertain and may vary with processing conditions and specific alloy systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples using identical processing and heat-treatment parameters: one set with the base composition (e.g. CrCoNiFe alloy) and one with an added 5–10 wt% Mo. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests, sustained load creep tests, and corrosion tests in a 3.5 wt% NaCl environment.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Creep displacement or strain rate under a defined sustained load and hold time at room temperature
Potentiodynamic polarization outputs (corrosion potential, corrosion current density)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-added HEA does not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., >10% increase in strength and reduction in creep displacement, along with better corrosion metrics) relative to the base alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHighly entropy alloys (HEAs) are novel materials that have great potential for application in aerospace and marine engineering due to their superior mechanical properties and benefits over conventional materials. NiCrCoFe, also referred to as Ni-based HEA, has exceptional low-temperature strength and microstructural stability. However, HEAs have limited corrosion resistance in some environments, such as a 3.5 wt% sodium chloride (NaCl) solution. Adding corrosion-resistant elements such as molybdenum (Mo) to HEAs is expected to increase their corrosion resistance in a variety of corrosive environments. Metal additive manufacturing reduces production times compared to casting and eliminates shrinkage issues, making it ideal for producing homogeneous HEA. This study used directed energy deposition (DED) to create Cr25-xCo25Ni25Fe25Mox (x = 0, 5, 10%) HEAs. Tensile strength and potentiodynamic polarization tests were used to assess the materials’ mechanical properties and corrosion resistance.
